title: Risotto alla Primavera
subtitle: Spring vegetable risotto with peas, asparagus, and broad beans
excerpt: Risotto alla primavera is a celebration of early spring: peas, asparagus tips, and broad beans stirred into a Parmesan risotto, finished with lots of butter and fresh herbs. It is the first green risotto of the year and tastes of the season changing.
sourceNotes: Primavera (spring) risotto is a modern concept that brings together the first vegetables of the season. Unlike the classic regional risotti that feature a single ingredient, this version celebrates abundance and is widely made across northern Italy in April and May.

content.text: Spring vegetable risotto works because the vegetables are added in stages: asparagus stems go in early so they cook through, asparagus tips go in at the end to stay bright green. Peas and broad beans go in in the last 5 minutes. The goal is to have everything just cooked when the rice is done.

items.prepNote: woody ends snapped off, tips separated from stems

content.text: Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Cook {{onion}} onion for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{carnaroli-rice}} rice and stir for 2 minutes. Pour in {{white-wine-dry}} wine and stir until absorbed.

Add hot {{vegetable-stock}} stock a ladleful at a time, stirring. After 8 minutes, add the {{asparagus}} asparagus stems. After 12 minutes, add {{peas-frozen}} peas and {{broad-beans}} broad beans. After 15 minutes, add the asparagus tips. Continue for 3 more minutes until the rice is al dente and the vegetables are just tender. Season with {{salt-table}} salt.
Remove from the heat. Stir in {{unsalted-butter}} butter and {{parmesan}} Parmesan vigorously. Add {{mint}} mint leaves and {{lemon}} lemon zest if using. Serve at once.

items.fix: Stage the vegetables by how long they take to cook. Asparagus stems take 8 minutes, peas and broad beans take 5 minutes, asparagus tips take only 3 minutes. Add them in reverse order of cooking time.

content.text: Spring risotto does not have the centuries-old pedigree of risotto alla Milanese or risi e bisi, but it has become one of the most popular spring dishes in Italian home cooking. It reflects what is available in April and May: the first asparagus, new peas, and young broad beans. The addition of mint and lemon zest at the finish is a modern touch that lightens the Parmesan richness.
